doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Conservatory education and making up for its gaps
summary: Piltzecker says Eastman did not give him a liberal arts education and he has been filling that in ever since.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well people have to find their own way to some extent anyway. I just sometimes worry about — I might have had the next you know really big player under my tutelage and I sort of took them on the broad path instead of the narrow path. Of course normally if I get a really, really good student, I tell them they need to go to somebody else if they get to a point where I can’t help you anymore.

Well yeah, we all should do it. It happens to me too, it’s great. Since we’re talking about education I’m going to a conservatory and it’s a bunch of race horse types, all trying to win you know, they really are taking it — involved with music and be, whatever. The skill will be moving all those great demands and be a fine musician. And most of the rewards, courses that I took as an undergraduate, were adequate to say the least. I mean there were a couple of wonderful professors that I had, but Eastman, that’s not what they do. And so I feel like I had to make up for that, for the rest of my life in a certain sense, so you know I’m still a student trying to read a little bit here and there and learn how life works and sort of fill out that liberal arts education, which a conservatory doesn’t really give you. In some curriculums, some five year programs exist that do that in certain places. But you know you can’t — what’s the right balance? What’s the right call for each individual? You don’t know that. But for me I’ve had to make up for that a little bit and it’s been joyous along the way, but there’s more to just being a great musician. I think it’s important to be many other things.
